claim: Gamma-band oscillations are implicated in modulation of attention, integration of sensory information and flexible communication among anatomically connected brain areas.
source: Gamma-band oscillations are implicated in modulation of attention, integration of sensory information and flexible communication among anatomically connected brain areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work in the field.

claim: Gamma frequency and amplitude can be modulated bi-directionally by phase-advancing or delaying optogenetic feedback to pyramidal cells.
source: Gamma frequency and amplitude can be modulated bi-directionally, and dissociated, by phase-advancing or delaying optogenetic feedback to pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Closed-loop modulation alters the synchrony rather than average frequency of action potentials.
source: Closed-loop modulation alters the synchrony rather than average frequency of action potentials, in principle avoiding disruption of population rate-coding of information.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cell-attached recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Modulation of phasic excitatory currents in principal neurons is sufficient to manipulate oscillations.
source: Modulation of phasic excitatory currents in principal neurons is sufficient to manipulate oscillations, suggesting that feed-forward excitation of pyramidal cells has an important role in determining oscillatory dynamics and the ability of networks to couple with one another.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: The CA1 subfield can flip between a state of coherence with the medial entorhinal cortex at ~110 Hz and a state of coherence with the CA3 subfield at ~40 Hz.
source: An earlier study in the rodent hippocampal formation showed that the CA1 subfield can flip between a state of coherence with the medial entorhinal cortex at ~110 Hz and a state of coherence with the CA3 subfield at ~40 Hz, correlating with information flow through the temporo-ammonic and Schaffer collateral pathways, respectively (Colgin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Colgin et al., 2009.

claim: Gamma-band oscillations can be induced in vitro in the presence of blockers of ionotropic glutamate receptors.
source: Gamma-band oscillations can be induced in vitro in the presence of blockers of ionotropic glutamate receptors (Whittington et al., 1995), or in vivo by optogenetic stimulation of parvalbumin-positive interneurons (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009), underlining the importance of fast perisomatic inhibition (Bartos et al., 2002; Fisahn et al., 2004; Mann et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Gamma-band oscillations can be entrained by sinusoidal optogenetic stimulation of pyramidal neurons in an in vitro hippocampal slice preparation.
source: Nevertheless, gamma-band oscillations can be entrained by sinusoidal optogenetic stimulation of pyramidal neurons in an in vitro hippocampal slice preparation (Akam et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Akam et al., 2012.

claim: Gamma in an in vitro hippocampal slice preparation shows a biphasic phase response curve (PRC).
source: The finding that gamma in an in vitro hippocampal slice preparation shows a biphasic PRC (Akam et al., 2012) is consistent with the hypothesis that this oscillation can be entrained by appropriately modulated afferent activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Akam et al., 2012.

claim: C1V1 was expressed in the mouse hippocampus CA1 under the Camk2a promoter to bias expression to excitatory neurons.
source: We expressed the red-shifted optogenetic actuator C1V1 (Yizhar et al., 2011) in the mouse hippocampus CA1 under the Camk2a promoter to bias expression to excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the experimental approach.

claim: A slowly increasing ramp of light (peak wavelength 590 nm) elicited a gamma oscillation in hippocampal slices.
source: A slowly increasing ramp of light (peak wavelength 590 nm) was delivered via a light-emitting diode (LED) coupled to the epifluorescence port of an upright microscope, eliciting a gamma oscillation (Figure 1a,b), as previously reported in rodents (Adesnik, 2018; Adesnik and Scanziani, 2010; Akam et al., 2012; Butler et al., 2016; Pastoll et al., 2013), cats (Ni et al., 2016) and monkeys (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: The LED driver command was multiplied by (1 + k1LFP + k2dLFP/dt) to achieve closed-loop modulation.
source: The LED driver command was multiplied by a simple function of the instantaneous value of the LFP and its time-derivative: (1 + k1 LFP + k2 dLFP/dt), where k1 and k2 are positive or negative constants.
evidence: This is a methodological description of the closed-loop approach.

claim: The gamma clamp had little effect on the average illumination intensity relative to an unmodulated ramp.
source: Because both the LFP and its time-derivative fluctuated about 0, the 'gamma clamp' had little effect on the average illumination intensity relative to an unmodulated ramp.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mathematical properties of the feedback function.

claim: In-phase modulation (k1 positive, k2 = 0) led to an increase in oscillatory power and frequency.
source: In-phase modulation, achieved by setting k1 positive and k2 = 0, led to an increase in oscillatory power and frequency (Figure 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Anti-phase modulation (k1 negative) led to a decrease in both frequency and power.
source: Modulating the ramp in anti-phase relative to the LFP, by setting k1 negative, led to a decrease in both frequency and power (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Phase-advancing the clamp by approximately 90° (k1 = 0, k2 positive) increased the frequency of the oscillation whilst decreasing its power.
source: Advancing the phase of the clamp by approximately 90°, achieved by setting k1 = 0 and k2 positive, increased the frequency of the oscillation whilst decreasing its power (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Delaying the trough of the clamp modulation relative to the LFP (k2 negative) resulted in a decrease in frequency and increase in power.
source: Finally, a decrease in frequency and increase in power was achieved by delaying the trough of the clamp modulation relative to the LFP, by setting k2 negative (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: With the appropriate phase of closed-loop feedback, the network oscillation could be pushed in any desired direction in the oscillation frequency-power space.
source: Moreover, as the LED-LFP phase difference was rotated through a complete cycle, the effect on the oscillation in the two-dimensional plane defined by the change in oscillation frequency and power also rotated through 360°, such that with the appropriate phase of closed-loop feedback the network oscillation could be pushed in any desired direction in the oscillation frequency-power space (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The characteristic relationship between frequency change and LED-LFP phase difference can be explained by the shape of the phase-response curve (PRC).
source: To gain a mechanistic insight, we asked if the characteristic relationship between the frequency change and the LED-LFP phase difference could be explained by the shape of the phase-response curve (PRC) previously reported (Akam et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior PRC data and comparison with current results.

claim: A phase delay was observed when the transient optogenetic stimulus was delivered at the trough of the LFP, when pyramidal neurons are most likely to fire.
source: A phase delay was observed when the transient optogenetic stimulus was delivered at the trough of the LFP, when pyramidal neurons are most likely to fire.
evidence: This claim refers to prior PRC data from Akam et al., 2012.

claim: The maximal phase advance occurred when the stimulus was delivered approximately one third of a cycle after the trough of the LFP.
source: The maximal phase advance, in contrast, occurred when the stimulus was delivered approximately one third of a cycle after the trough of the LFP.
evidence: This claim refers to prior PRC data from Akam et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibitory currents in principal neurons are the main determinant of the LFP.
source: Inhibitory currents in principal neurons, rather than spikes or excitatory currents, have previously been shown to be the main determinant of the LFP (Oren et al., 2010), suggesting that the change in power during the clamp is not a direct effect of the optogenetic drive but results instead from a change in pyramidal neuron synchrony or phase, in a reciprocal relationship with the degree and temporal synchrony of interneuron recruitment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oren et al., 2010 and inference about the mechanism.

claim: During an unmodulated ramp, pyramidal cells tended to spike sparsely, close to the trough of the oscillation.
source: During an unmodulated ramp, pyramidal cells tended to spike sparsely, close to the trough of the oscillation, consistent with previous studies of pharmacologically induced oscillations (Fisahn et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: An increase in oscillatory power was associated with a corresponding increase in the degree of synchrony of pyramidal cell firing.
source: During the clamp, an increase in oscillatory power was associated with a corresponding increase in the degree of synchrony of pyramidal cell firing: the circular dispersion of LFP phase at which pyramidal cells fired decreased relative to the unclamped situation (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: A decrease in power was accompanied by a relative desynchronization of pyramidal cell firing.
source: Conversely, a decrease in power was accompanied by a relative desynchronization of pyramidal cell firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The vector length increased when oscillation power increased (p=0.02, n = 12).
source: The vector length increased when oscillation power increased (p=0.02, n = 12, sign test), and decreased when oscillation power decreased (p=0.025, n = 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no change in the overall firing rate of pyramidal cells when the oscillation power was increased or decreased by the clamp.
source: Strikingly, however, there was no change in the overall firing rate of pyramidal cells when the oscillation power was increased or decreased by the clamp.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Changes in power were achieved by tightening the synchrony of firing, or by desynchronizing action potentials, rather than by altering the overall activity of pyramidal neurons.
source: Changes in power were thus achieved by tightening the synchrony of firing, or by desynchronizing action potentials, rather than by altering the overall activity of pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that firing rate did not change while synchrony did.

claim: Increases in oscillatory frequency were accompanied by a phase advance of pyramidal cell firing relative to the LFP (p=8×10−7, n = 7).
source: Increases in oscillatory frequency were accompanied by a phase advance of pyramidal cell firing relative to the LFP (Figure 4b,c, p=8×10−7, n = 7, Hotellier test – Zar, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Changes in the phase of pyramidal neuron action potentials are causally upstream of changes in gamma frequency.
source: This observation is consistent with the view that changes in the phase of pyramidal neuron action potentials are causally upstream of changes in gamma frequency, even though the current generators of the LFP itself are dominated by GABAergic signaling (Gulyás et al., 2010; Hájos et al., 2004; Oren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations and citations to prior work.

claim: During unclamped gamma, the excitatory current was small, and its average phase relative to the LFP varied among experiments.
source: During unclamped gamma, the excitatory current was small, and its average phase relative to the LFP varied among experiments, as expected from the very sparse synaptic connectivity among pyramidal neurons in CA1 (Deuchars and Thomson, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: Gamma clamp imposed a large phasic inward current.
source: Gamma clamp imposed a large phasic inward current (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The net excitatory current imposed by gamma clamp lagged behind the LED modulation, reflecting in part the opsin activation and deactivation kinetics.
source: Subtracting the vector representing the baseline phasic inward current yielded a vector representing the net excitatory current imposed by the gamma clamp (ΔE). This lagged behind the LED modulation, reflecting in part the opsin activation and deactivation kinetics (Figure 5c, and arrows in Figure 5b, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and inference about opsin kinetics.

claim: An increase in gamma frequency was achieved when the average excitatory current phase occurred during the down-stroke of the LFP (~180° to 360°).
source: An increase in gamma frequency was achieved when the average excitatory current phase occurred during the down-stroke of the LFP (~180° to 360°), whilst a decrease in frequency was achieved when excitation was applied during the upstroke (~0° to 180°).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: An increase in power was achieved with excitation around the trough (~270° to 90°), and a decrease in power occurred with excitation around the peak (~90° to 270°).
source: An increase in power, on the other hand, was achieved with excitation around the trough (~270° to 90°), and a decrease in power occurred with excitation around the peak (~90° to 270°).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The increase in frequency occurs because pyramidal neurons are brought to firing threshold earlier.
source: Given that, under baseline conditions, pyramidal neurons fire maximally near to the trough of the LFP (0°), these data imply that the increase in frequency occurs because they are brought to firing threshold earlier (see also Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between excitation phase and firing timing.

claim: An increase in power occurs because pyramidal neurons are synchronized by adding a depolarization when they are most likely to fire.
source: An increase in power, on the other hand, occurs because pyramidal neurons are synchronized by adding a depolarization when they are most likely to fire (see also Figure 4a,c).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between excitation phase and synchrony.

claim: Phasic inhibitory currents under baseline conditions were large, consistent with the major role of feedback interneurons in gamma.
source: In contrast to excitatory currents, phasic inhibitory currents under baseline conditions were large, consistent with the major role of feedback interneurons in gamma (Figure 7a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and established knowledge about gamma mechanisms.

claim: Changes in inhibitory currents (ΔI) were relatively smaller than for excitatory currents and were dominated by effects on the power of the oscillation.
source: Changes in inhibitory currents (ΔI) were relatively smaller than for excitatory currents and were dominated by effects on the power of the oscillation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Closed-loop optogenetic manipulation of principal cells allows predictable, bidirectional and dissociable changes in the power and frequency of gamma oscillations.
source: The present study shows that closed-loop optogenetic manipulation of principal cells allows predictable, bidirectional and dissociable changes in the power and frequency of gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is a summary claim of the main findings supported by all experimental data.

claim: There was broad consistency between the frequency manipulation achieved with closed-loop optogenetic feedback and that predicted from the phase response behavior previously observed with intermittent optogenetic stimuli.
source: We observed a broad consistency between the frequency manipulation achieved with closed-loop optogenetic feedback and that predicted from the phase response behavior previously observed with intermittent optogenetic stimuli (Akam et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison between current results and prior PRC data.

claim: The principles uncovered in the present work are not specific to the way gamma oscillations were elicited.
source: Optogenetically and pharmacologically induced gamma also exhibited similar dynamical properties in that study, implying that the principles uncovered in the present work are not specific to the way gamma oscillations were elicited.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with prior work showing similar PRC properties.

claim: PV+ basket cells tend to fire with very little phase dispersion, close to one-to-one with each cycle of the oscillation in vitro.
source: PV+ basket cells tend to fire with very little phase dispersion, close to one-to-one with each cycle of the oscillation in vitro (Bartos et al., 2007; Gulyás et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Attempts to achieve gamma clamp by targeting interneurons rather than pyramidal cells have been unsuccessful because their out of phase recruitment powerfully suppresses the oscillation.
source: Our attempts to achieve gamma clamp by targeting interneurons rather than pyramidal cells have thus far been unsuccessful because their out of phase recruitment powerfully suppresses the oscillation (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished experimental observations.

claim: The weaker phase-locking of pyramidal than PV+ cell firing to gamma oscillations may confer a broader dynamic range over which they can influence the phase, frequency and amplitude of the oscillation.
source: The weaker phase-locking of pyramidal than PV+ cell firing to gamma oscillations, together with their sparse firing on successive cycles of gamma (Csicsvari et al., 2003; Gulyás et al., 2010; Tukker et al., 2007), may however confer a broader dynamic range over which they can influence the phase, frequency and amplitude of the oscillation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on known properties of pyramidal cell firing and the current results.

claim: The present data underline the importance of action potential timing in principal cells in the spectral and temporal properties of hippocampal gamma.
source: Taken together with previous evidence that open-loop sinusoidal optogenetic stimulation of principal cells can entrain a gamma oscillation (Akam et al., 2012), the present data underline the importance of action potential timing in principal cells in the spectral and temporal properties of hippocampal gamma, notwithstanding the evidence that the LFP itself is dominated by inhibitory currents in principal cells (Oren et al., 2010), and argue against a model where the function of principal cells is only to depolarize a population of reciprocally connected interneurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current results and prior work.

claim: The ability to alter the amplitude and frequency of gamma suggests a versatile tool to test the roles of gamma in information routing and other high-level brain functions.
source: The ability to alter the amplitude and frequency of gamma suggests a versatile tool to test the roles of gamma in information routing and other high-level brain functions, both in health and in disease states such as schizophrenia (Uhlhaas and Singer, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential applications of the technique.

claim: External periodic stimulation is not well suited to desynchronize network activity or to suppress oscillatory dynamics.
source: However, external periodic stimulation is not well suited to desynchronize network activity or to suppress oscillatory dynamics.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the limitations of periodic stimulation.

claim: If periodic stimulation is used, the desired change in amplitude or frequency is achieved at the cost of imposing an externally determined phase on the oscillation.
source: Furthermore, if periodic stimulation is used, the desired change in amplitude or frequency is achieved at the cost of imposing an externally determined phase on the oscillation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the properties of periodic stimulation.

claim: Closed-loop manipulation of a gamma oscillation can be achieved without a net increase or decrease in the average firing rate of neurons.
source: We have, moreover, shown that closed-loop manipulation of a gamma oscillation can be achieved without a net increase or decrease in the average firing rate of neurons, implying that it would not necessarily perturb information represented as an average firing rate code.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Optogenetics has the advantage over electrical stimulation that the modulation can be distributed across a population of neurons.
source: Importantly, optogenetics has the advantage over electrical stimulation that the modulation can be distributed across a population of neurons.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the properties of optogenetics.

claim: P21 male C57 mice were used for viral injections.
source: P21 male C57 mice were anesthetized with isoflurane and placed in a stereotaxic frame (Kopf Instruments).
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: AAV5-CaMKIIa-C1V1(E122T/E162T)-TS-eYFP was injected at a rate of 100 nl/min into four sites in both hippocampi.
source: A suspension of AAV5-CaMKIIa-C1V1(E122T/E162T)-TS-eYFP (UNC Vector Core, titre 5 × 1012 IU/ml) was injected at a rate of 100 nl/min into four sites in both hippocampi (injection volume: 300–500 nl per site).
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: Hippocampal slices were prepared at least 4 weeks after viral injection.
source: Hippocampal slices were prepared at least 4 weeks later.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: Brain slices were 400 μm thick.
source: Brain slices (400 μm thick) were prepared at room temperature and then incubated at 37°C for 12 min in the same solution.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: CA3 was ablated to focus on local gamma-generating mechanisms.
source: Expression of C1V1 in CA1 was verified by epifluorescence, and CA3 was ablated to focus on local gamma-generating mechanisms.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: The irradiance was <5 mW/mm2.
source: The current delivered to the LED was kept in the linear input-output range, and the irradiance was <5 mW/mm2.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: Light ramps typically lasted 8 s and were delivered every 30 – 45 s.
source: Light ramps typically lasting 8 s were delivered every 30 – 45 s.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: LFPs were band-pass filtered between 1 and 200 or 500 Hz.
source: LFPs were recorded in the CA1 pyramidal layer using patch pipettes filled with extracellular solution and a Multiclamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices), and band-pass filtered between 1 and 200 or 500 Hz.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: The FPGA operated at a loop rate of 10 kHz.
source: A linear LED ramp command was generated via a multifunction data acquisition card (National Instruments PCI-6221) and, together with the LFP, was digitized using a real-time controller (National Instruments cRIO-9022) with a Xilinx Virtex-5 FPGA (cRIO-9133) operating at a loop rate of 10 kHz.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: dLFP/dt was calculated as the difference between successive digitization values in the FPGA, averaged over successive 2 ms intervals to minimize high-frequency noise.
source: dLFP/dt was calculated as the difference between successive digitization values in the FPGA, averaged over successive 2 ms intervals to minimize high-frequency noise.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: Phasic conductances were estimated from Ohm's law, assuming a driving force of 70 mV.
source: Phasic conductances (Figure 7d) were estimated from Ohm's law, assuming a driving force of 70 mV.
evidence: This is a methodological description.

claim: Gamma cycles that deviated more than 20% from the modal period were rejected.
source: Gamma cycles that deviated more than 20% from the modal period were rejected.
evidence: This is a methodological description of data analysis.
